> > M=250

> > psi=0.4
> > Tmax=10
> > z <- rbinom(M, 1, psi )                               # True Occupancy
> > t.rand <- rexp(M, rate = lambda)               # Random Time to First Detection based on lambda

> > time.det <- ifelse(t.rand <= Tmax & z == 1, t.rand, NA)              # Observed Time to First Detection. Perhaps round if time units finite.
d <- as.numeric(is.na <http://is.na>(time.det))    # Censoring indicator
hist(time.det, breaks=50)

# 10.12.1 Occupancy models with "survival model" observation process:
#         exponential time-to-detection (TTD) model with simulated data

modelstring="
model{
# Priors
int.psi ~ dunif(0, 1)               # Intercept occupancy on prob. scale
int.lambda ~ dgamma(0.0001, 0.0001) # Poisson rate parameter
beta1~dnorm(0,0.001)
alpha1~dnorm(0,0.001)
# Likelihood
for (i in 1:nobs){
# Model for occurrence
z[i] ~ dbern(psi[i])
logit(psi[i])<-logit(int.psi+beta1)
#logit(psi[i])<-logit(int.psi)                #without beta

# Observation model
# Exponential model for time to detection ignoring censoring
ttd[i] ~ dexp(lambda[i])
log(lambda[i])<-log(int.lambda+alpha1)
#log(lambda[i])<-log(int.lambda)             #without alpha
# Model for censoring due to species absence and ttd>=Tmax
d[i] ~ dbern(theta[i])                                             #d <- as.numeric(is.na <http://is.na>(data$ttd))    # Censoring indicator
theta[i] <- z[i] * step(ttd[i] - Tmax) + (1 - z[i])
}
# Derived quantities
n.occ <- sum(z[])                   # Number of occupied sites
}
"
writeLines(modelstring, con="model.txt")

A couple things to try:
Use normal priors for int.psi, int.lambda, beta1, and alpha1.
logit(psi[i])<- int.psi+beta1 * data.beta1[i]                     # you require data for your covariate, or remove the term beta1.  Also you don't want 'logit' on both sides of your equation.
lambda[i] <- exp(int.lambda + alpha1 * data.alpha[i])   # you require data for your covariate, or remove the term alpha1.  Also don't want the 'log' transformation on both sides of your equation.

Hope this helps,
Jesse

messages.body_plain:
Dear unmarked users,

We're extremely pleased to announce a new release of unmarked -- version 0.12-3 (on CRAN as of yesterday).

We have a number of small changes, enhancements and bug fixes thanks to Richard, Mike Meredith, Adam Smith, Chris Baker.
For the specifics you can check out the GitHub here: https://github.com/rbchan/unmarked/commits/master

The Big NEW ADDITON, thanks to a massive effort by Ken Kellner and Chris Rota, is the implementation of multispecies occupancy models -- see the function occuMulti and ?occuMulti.  This implements the models of Rota et al. (2016). This is an important class of models and we're excited to have this functionality in unmarked.

We will include a vignette for occuFP in some minor update soon (thanks to Chris Sutherland).

Apologies for the slow update cycle of unmarked. This is sure to continue at least until AHM2 is finished and out the door (this spring). I hope someday we can advance unmarked's capabilities at a faster rate.  We still have dreams to include open distance sampling models and multi-state occupancy models. When these two things are done, I will retire.

Thanks everyone!
regards,
Andy and Richard

messages.body_plain:
Dear Geraldine,

in your parboot, new data sets are simulated under your model, using the parameters estimated from your actual data set. Each replicate data set is then analysed using the same model, and, using the same value of K.

The error message seems to indicate that for some simulated data set, the maximum count was larger than 200. This may seem strange, but you have a NegBin distibution, which produces such extreme counts more often than the Poisson. So, you have to repeat the analysis of the actual data set with a K that is larger, such that it is large enough for ALL simulated data sets.

Different thing: Have you checked whether your estimates are stable when you increase K ? Such sensitivity of the estimates to K is a frequent problem with NegBin mixtures for the static Nmix model and I could imagine it also happens in the dynamic Nmix (i.e., Dail-Madsen).

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jody,

I think Jim's first instinct might be right--it doesn't seem possible that the model is identifiable with one 'site', and I think this is why the occuRN function expects multiple rows.  I think you're getting an answer that depends upon where you choose to stop the integration over the latent abundance state and where you end up starting the optimizer.

library(unmarked)
y<-matrix(NA, 2, 50)
y[1, ]<-rbinom(50, 1, 1-(1-.2)^5) ##N is 5, r = 0.2
UMF<-unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y)
rn<-occuRN(~1 ~1, UMF)
predict(rn, "state")
rn2<-occuRN(~1 ~1, UMF, K=100)
rn2_5<-occuRN(~1 ~1, UMF, K=100, starts=c(2, -3))
rn2_5_5<-occuRN(~1 ~1, UMF, K=100, starts=c(0, 1))
predict(rn2, "state")
predict(rn2_5, "state")
predict(rn2_5_5, "state")
rn3<-occuRN(~1 ~1, UMF, K=1000)
predict(rn3, "state")

The model needs some 'site' replication to tease the state/detection processes apart. That said, there's some wiggle room w/r/t how sites are defined---here's an example  <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/j.1365-2664.2010.01922.x>where different years at one site are treated as different 'sites'', and splitting your sampling periods up *might* be one way to tackle this. (Another way might be to treat each species as a 'site'', although this also raises a different set of issues). If you have recorded times of detection, or distances, there might be better options available to you.

I've attached a write-up which suggests (as does John Clare) that either the model is not identifiable or it is "nearly not identifiable" (a term that I obviously made up).  Here is the first part of the write-up:

Jody found an ingenious work-around for getting occuRN to produce estimates and standard errors when there is but a single site by adding in a second row of NA values.  However, while Jody’s approach does produce results, these are not the values of the maximum likelihood estimates.

But following Jody’s lead by having the second row of data being a duplicate of the first row (instead of putting in NA’s) gets one the maximum likelihood estimates with the standard errors inflated by a multiplicative factor of the square root of 2 if the starting values are close enough to the maximum likelihood estimates.

First the logic:  By having two rows of identical data just doubles the log of the likelihood (or squares the likelihood).  Therefore, the values that maximize twice the log of the likelihood will not have changed from using the log of the likelihood for a single site.  This also implies that the resulting variances will be underestimated by a multiplicative factor of 2.
A teaser:  Below I suggest that for a single site maximum likelihood estimates are useless.

And here is a look at the log likelihood surface when T=17, w=10, and K=100:

messages.body_plain:
Hey Chance,

I've run into a similar problem when using unmarked. I think there are a few pieces that are tripping you up here. The first is that you should give linearComb a vector of numbers not characters. Here's an example with some simulated data:

library(unmarked)
library(AHMbook)

# Generate some distance data using a function from AHMbook
sim_out <- simHDS("line", nsites=100, mean.sigma = 2, show.plot=F)

# Tidy things up so it works well enough with the format function
data <- data.frame(sim_out$data)
data$site <- factor(data$site, levels=as.character(seq(1,100,1) ) )

# Format the data for input into unmarked
yDat <- formatDistData(data, distCol = "d", transectNameCol = "site",
                       dist.breaks = seq(0, 3, 0.5))

# Make some fake habitat categories
habitat <- rep( c("A", "B", "C", "D"), each=25)

# Put this in a data frame
covs <- data.frame(hab=factor(habitat))

# Run things like Chance

umf <- unmarkedFrameDS(y=as.matrix(yDat), siteCovs=covs,survey="line",

                       dist.breaks=seq(0, 3, 0.5), tlength=rep(3000, 100),
                       unitsIn="m")

hn_Hab.Ht2 <- distsamp(~1 ~hab, keyfun="halfnorm", umf)

Then you can use linearComb to figure out what the average abundance is in habitat A. You just put in a 1 for a covariate class you want included and a 0 for one you don't. The covariate order is the same as what's listed in the model output. You can wrap backTransform around this too like you were trying to do in your earlier code.

linearComb(hn_Hab.Ht2, coefficients = c(1, 0, 0, 0), type = 'state')

The post you referenced before was looking for a way to get those nice p-values for all combinations of covariates.

You could do something like this:

covs$hab <- factor(covs$hab, levels=c("B", "A", "C", "D"))

umf <- unmarkedFrameDS(y=as.matrix(yDat), siteCovs=covs,survey="line",

                       dist.breaks=seq(0, 3, 0.5), tlength=rep(3000, 100),
                       unitsIn="m")

hn_Hab.Ht2 <- distsamp(~1 ~hab, keyfun="halfnorm", umf)

Where you change the order of factor levels so that you're contrasting abundance/density in A, C, and D habitats against B. You can also do the same with relevel but it looks a little uglier. Basically you're telling R to consider habitat "A" in the example below as the intercept, you can change it to whatever category you like.

hn_Hab.Ht2 <- distsamp(~1 ~relevel(hab, "A"), keyfun="halfnorm", umf)

Hopefully that helps some and hopefully I haven't given any spurious advice.

-Jerry

Here’s another solution, to complement Jerry’s suggestions. This is for an N-mixture model, but the approach should be fairly generic.
## Simulate data from model: y~Bin(N,p); N~Pois(lam) where
## lam is function one factor with 3 levels

dat <- data.frame(x1=gl(3,30, labels=LETTERS[1:3]))
dat

nSites <- nrow(dat)

X <- model.matrix(~x1, dat) # design matrix
beta <- c(-1, 1, 2)         # coefficients of the log-linear model
lam <- exp(X %*% beta)      # expected value of abundance at each site

N <- rpois(nSites, lam)             # site-specific abundance
y <- matrix(rbinom(n*4, N, 0.5), n) # repeated count data

## Fit model in unmarked
library(unmarked)
umf <- unmarkedFramePCount(y=y, siteCovs=dat)

fm1 <- pcount(~1 ~x1, umf, K=100)
fm1

## Create dummy coefficients for each level of the factor.
## These would need to be modified if there are other covariates in the model or if there are not 3 levels of the factor.
xA <- c(1, 0, 0)
xB <- c(1, 1, 0)
xC <- c(1, 0, 1)

## Compare A vs B
## Test null hypothesis that mean abundance in level A is
## equal to mean abundance in level B (on the log scale)
AvB <- linearComb(fm1, xA-xB, type="state")
AvB
confint(AvB)

## Compare A vs C
## Test null hypothesis that mean abundance in level A is
## equal to mean abundance in level C (on the log scale)
AvC <- linearComb(fm1, xA-xC, type="state")
AvC
confint(AvC)

## Compare B vs C
## Test null hypothesis that mean abundance in level B is
## equal to mean abundance in level C (on the log scale)
BvC <- linearComb(fm1, xB-xC, type="state")
BvC
confint(BvC)

messages.body_plain:
Good afternoon,

I am building dynamic occupancy models to understand factors that drive annual and seasonal shifts in red-headed woodpecker habitat use.  The model I am working on currently uses point count data collected during the summers of 2016 and 2017 (2 primary periods).

I started with simple models and added covariates in a stepwise fashion, comparing AIC scores at each stage.  First, I added covariates for detection (p), then initial occupancy (psi), then colonization (gamma).  Eventually, I would fit covariates for the extinction parameter (epsilon), but I ran into trouble while fitting covariates for colonization (gamma):

# Colonization (gamma)
Fm0 <- colext(~PrOpen + st_dens + snags + burn, ~1, ~1, ~wind, data = umf)
Fm1 <- colext(~PrOpen + st_dens + snags + burn, ~st_dens, ~1, ~wind, data = umf)
Fm2 <- colext(~PrOpen + st_dens + snags + burn, ~mast, ~1, ~wind, data = umf)
Fm3 <- colext(~PrOpen + st_dens + snags + burn, ~pines, ~1, ~wind, data = umf)
Fm4 <- colext(~PrOpen + st_dens + snags + burn, ~snags, ~1, ~wind, data = umf)
Fm5 <- colext(~PrOpen + st_dens + snags + burn, ~W, ~1, ~wind, data = umf)
Fm6 <- colext(~PrOpen + st_dens + snags + burn, ~SDI, ~1, ~wind, data = umf)

Hi Tam

I work with camera traps in estimating abundance and density of two mammal species and I work with detection histories generated with package camtrapR, and this is the route to enter the data in occupancy models, these links could be usefull to you:

http://www.revmexmastozoologia.unam.mx/ojs/index.php/rmm/article/view/245
https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/camtrapR/vignettes/DataExtraction.html

For occuRN the data you have to use are detection histories of your species, due that this models work with detection/ not detection data, for each site and survey period. In case of N-mixture models the data to use are counts, but is important that you inspect if your records meet the assumptions of this models.

You can take a look of this book to undesrstand general concepts of models:
https://www.elsevier.com/books/applied-hierarchical-modeling-in-ecology-analysis-of-distribution-abundance-and-species-richness-in-r-and-bugs/kery/978-0-12-801378-6

Best regards,

Karen

In the mb.gof.test() code, try making a small change to the parboot call to turn off parallel processing. Change this:

mb.gof.test.RN <- function (mod, nsim = 5, plot.hist = TRUE, ...){
  mod.table <- mb.chisq.RN(mod)

                 nsim = nsim)
  p.value <- sum(ou...@t.star >= out@t0)/nsim

to this:

mb.gof.test.RN <- function (mod, nsim = 5, plot.hist = TRUE, ...){
  mod.table <- mb.chisq.RN(mod)
  out <- parboot(mod, statistic = function(i) mb.chisq.RN(i)$chi.square,
                 nsim = nsim, parallel=FALSE)
  p.value <- sum(ou...@t.star >= out@t0)/nsim

I think the mb.chisq.RN function is not being properly exported into the parallel cluster (which only activates when nsim > 100). This is just a guess, without an example I can't test it.

Ken
